newsitem.title: ITALY: Storms ahead for Prodi a year after Italy poll win.
newsitem.headline: Storms ahead for Prodi a year after Italy poll win.

text.p: Worries about the stability of Italy's centre-left coalition re-surfaced over the weekend as commentators looked back on Prime Minister Romano Prodi's first year in power.

Prodi has formally been in office 11 months -- about the average life span, co-incidentally, of Italy's legion of post-war governments -- but his hopes of making history by reaching anything like a full term have been dented in recent weeks.
Since last Spring, the government has been through 19 parliamentary confidence votes, seen allies vote against it and drawn the opposition of business leaders.
Popular support for the Olive Tree coalition has been tempered by increased taxation to meet targets for the European single currency.
Political analysts expect local elections next Sunday in 1,138 towns including Milan and Turin to give an indication of how far grass roots support has been eroded.

"Lacerated by profound disagreements between the forces backing it, Prodi's government may not even be around to celebrate its first birthday," the far-right National Alliance leader Gianfranco Fini commented at the weekend.
His words bore a dose of wishful thinking but the internal discord has become increasingly evident.

In the past month alone, the government has run into trouble over a proposed mini-budget designed to reduce the deficit and keep Italy on course for membership of the European single currency from the start in January 1999.
Business leaders, angered by measures bringing forward certain tax payments by companies, and the centre-right opposition have asked for it to be withdrawn.
"Not a week goes by without something happening." said Prodi. "But we are moving forward, things are getting done".
Europe, and meeting the strict criteria for joining economic and monetary union (EMU) has been the overriding priority of Prodi's government from the outset.
That factor has ensured solidarity so far, with politicians wary of losing out on Europe by prompting a crisis.

In many areas significant strides have been made, with Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi saying last week that he expected April consumer price inflation figures to come in at 1.8 percent year-on-year, the lowest since 1969.
The Bank of Italy has cut its discount rate three times in the past 10 months, bringing the rate down to 6.75 percent from nine percent in early July 1996.
And the European Commission last week forecast that Italy's budget deficit would hit 3.2 percent of gross domestic product, outside the single currency target but down from 6.7 percent in 1996.

However commentators have warned that relying on the hard-left Communist Refoundation for a majority in the lower house has tied the government's hands, particularly in negotiating the thorny subject of pension reform.

Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini added to pressure at the weekend when he called for reforms to be set out by June and suggested that if Refoundation proved intransigent, the coalition should move further to the centre.
Refoundation rocked Prodi's government last week when they voted against plans to send an Italian-led multi-national force to Albania. The opposition helped carry the motion.
"At the moment we face the risk that the coalition may not hold," Dini warned in northern Italy on Saturday.
Commentators have also become increasingly critical.

"A lot of Italians say that Prodi's time is just about up. Their judgement may, of course be premature. But the list of failures behind and problems in front is beginning to lengthen," wrote the Economist magazine last week.

Prominent commentator Sergio Romano wrote in La Stampa newspaper on Sunday that "the government wants Italy to participate in monetary union from the first day and makes that objective the very reason for its existence."
"To achieve those aims, the Prodi government has now become an obstacle," he concluded.
